title: The Path to Efficient Energy Use: Understanding Industry Maturity Levels
text:
## The Path to Efficient Energy Use: Understanding Industrial Maturity Levels

## Introduction

• According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), the industry sector was directly responsible for emitting 9.0 gigatonnes (Gt) of CO2 in 2022, accounting for a quarter of global energy system CO2 emissions. Although there have been modest advancements in energy efficiency and the adoption of renewable energy—and some positive strides in international collaboration and innovation—progress remains slow. Achieving meaningful milestones toward the net-zero emissions (NZE) by 2030 scenario requires more substantial improvements. This includes enhancing material and energy efficiency, accelerating the adoption of low-carbon fuels, and expediting the development and deployment of nearly zero-emission production processes. 
• Consequently, energy efficiency and management is becoming critically 

important in manufacturing. With rising energy costs and increasing environmental concerns, manufacturers are looking for ways to reduce energy consumption and meet sustainability targets. Managing energy consumption effectively not only helps industrial companies to reduce energy costs, but it also contributes to a more sustainable way of doing business.

• In 2023, Rockwell Automation commissioned Omdia to conduct an online survey to better understand where the industry is on its energy management journey, and to support an industry energy calculator. This white paper presents some of the key findings from the survey, and addresses topics such as key drivers, inhibitors, and challenges, and how companies can overcome these to deliver their targets. 

### The importance of monitoring and managing energy consumption in manufacturing

### Where is the industry today?

• The Omdia survey highlights considerable differences in maturity level when it comes to overall energy reduction programs for the production process. 
• Some companies are more advanced, i.e., they have fully deployed solutions across multiple facilities (31%). These manufacturers have clearly outlined strategies and have implemented digital tools to support the optimization of energy consumption. Other companies are at the proof of concept (PoC) stage/ in development (26%). 
• However, the majority of companies surveyed (43%) are somewhere in between: they have deployed energy reduction programs at individual sites, but may not have a centralized program in place. For companies with multiple facilities, this can cause challenges, e.g., coordinating energy contracts.

## Challenges to introducing effective energy management

### Barriers to effective energy management

A key challenge to effective energy management implementation is the tendency to focus on the technical solution in isolation, without considering the importance of people’s skillsets and expertise, and organizational commitment from top management. Some of the barriers that inhibit organizational ability to manage energy may include factors such as legacy assets, lack of access to energy data, lack of data visibility, lack of benchmark/baseline metrics, inadequate skillsets and expertise, and competing priorities.

• Legacy assets: Many facilities have equipment that is decades old. This creates two challenges: as equipment ages it tends to wear and run less efficiently; and legacy equipment has often not been designed with connectivity in mind, limiting access to data. 
• Lack of access to energy data: When it comes to measuring water, air, gas, energy, and steam (WAGES) usage, many companies do not have access to energy data in real time through their machinery and equipment. This is often linked to legacy devices or networking architecture. Access to energy data is not just about the production environment but it is also important at the utility level. Companies therefore need to effectively integrate the two to optimize energy usage. 
• Inadequate skillsets and expertise: There is often a skills gap when it comes to understanding energy data. This is partly due to a lack of focused job roles, as staff take on dual responsibilities, including but not limited to energy management. For example, it could be a digital role with an added responsibility for sustainability. 
• Lack of organizational commitment: A fundamental aspect of an organization’s energy management effectiveness is its commitment. Improving energy management is crucial to increased profitability, less dependence on non sustainable resources, and reduced environmental impact. Too often energy is treated as a crisis problem, whereas energy management requires constant and full attention to be effective. 
• Competing priorities: Examples of competing priorities could include production wanting to maximize output without considering energy consumption, or product design creating a product that uses sustainable materials but consumes more energy in production. 

## Why should industrial companies care about energy management?

### Why should companies care about energy management?

• Cost savings: The industrial sector is one of the main consumers of energy. It accounted for 37% of global energy use in 2022, while the US industrial sector accounted for 33% of total US energy consumption in the same year. Industrial energy management solutions can help plant and energy managers identify areas where energy waste can be reduced, and unnecessary energy consumption can be eliminated. This can lead to significant cost savings over time, and improved plant performance and sustainability. 
• Reduced emissions: The manufacturing sector accounted for one-fifth of global carbon emissions and 54% of the world’s energy usage in 2022. Reducing carbon emissions from the manufacturing sector will play a vital role in reaching global climate targets. For manufacturers, the benefits of carbon management extend beyond sustainability. Manufacturers that effectively manage their carbon emissions will stay compliant with existing and future legislation, minimize waste, and increase efficiency. 
• Energy security: The IEA defines energy security as the uninterrupted availability of energy sources at an affordable price. There are many aspects to energy security. Long-term energy security mainly deals with timely investments to supply energy in line with economic developments and environmental needs. On the other hand, short-term energy security focuses on the energy system’s ability to react promptly to sudden changes in the supply/demand balance. While the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 did not initiate the current energy supply crisis, it raised attention to the ongoing issues. The recent energy crisis has also accelerated the legislation process further and necessitated efforts to safeguard supply security. Industrial companies can address energy security through diversifying energy sources, investing in renewable energy, improving energy efficiency, and developing new energy technologies. 

## Introducing the stages of maturity

### Stages of maturity - Devices and metering

Where is the market today? The Omdia survey shows that 56% of respondents use meters for measuring at a production line level (27%) or use siloed/unconnected meters for individual assets (30%). Where factories are digitized, meters tend to be installed at the production line, which is separate to the utilities of the factory. When it comes to measuring electricity usage, many companies do not have access to energy sources in real time through their machinery and equipment. What can companies do to move to the next level? Companies can focus on network connectivity and communications between the utility and production level to progress to the next level. With factories becoming more digitalized, energy can be monitored at the equipment level to generate data for further analysis. Companies should aim to have real-time access to data, both at the utility and production level, in order to effectively optimize energy usage.

### Stages of maturity - Energy auditing

Where is the market today? The Omdia survey shows that almost 90% of respondents currently carry out energy audits. Of these, the majority conduct energy survey and analysis and targeted energy audits (47%); followed by detailed energy audits of capital-intensive modifications (25%), the most comprehensive approach; and walk-through energy audits (17%), the least comprehensive approach. What can companies do to move to the next level? Plant and equipment are often the largest consumers of energy in manufacturing. Auditing plant and machinery can highlight areas of significant energy consumption throughout different processes and potential opportunities for savings. The key factors to consider are the sources of energy use; energy consumption of each item of equipment; past and present energy usage; and current performance of facilities, systems, and processes.
